findings.title: OAuth token exchange failure is not handled, causing unhandled exception instead of user-facing error
findings.body: In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, `safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` is called without any exception handling. If GitHub's token endpoint returns a non-2xx status (e.g., invalid/expired/replayed `code`, rate limiting, or network error), `safe_urlopen` raises an exception that propagates up as a 500 error rather than the intended user-facing 'Invalid installation request' error page. The PR description explicitly states the pipeline should fail gracefully when 'GitHub could not generate correct access_token from the code (wrong or attempt of re-use of code)', but a GitHub error response (which is the normal way GitHub signals a bad code) will crash instead of rendering the error template. The subsequent try/except only wraps `safe_urlread(req).decode('utf-8')` and `parse_qsl`, not the `safe_urlopen` call itself, so HTTP error statuses from the token endpoint are unhandled.

findings.title: OAuth authorize redirect URL parameters are not URL-encoded
findings.body: The redirect to GitHub's authorize endpoint is built via f-string interpolation: `f"{ghip.get_oauth_authorize_url()}?client_id={github_client_id}&state={state}&redirect_uri={redirect_uri}"`. The `redirect_uri` value (produced by `absolute_uri(reverse(...))`) and potentially `state` are not URL-encoded with `urlencode`. If `redirect_uri` contains characters like `&`, `=`, `+`, or spaces (e.g., from a customer-domain URL prefix or unusual host configuration), the query string will be malformed — parameters can be injected or truncated, potentially causing the OAuth flow to use an incorrect redirect_uri or allowing parameter manipulation. This should use `urllib.parse.urlencode` to safely construct the query string.

findings.title: User mismatch check crashes with KeyError when integration metadata lacks 'sender'
findings.body: In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, the check `pipeline.fetch_state("github_authenticated_user") != integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` accesses `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` directly. However, `sender` is only populated in `build_integration` when `state.get("sender")` is present (line 376-377), and `build_integration` is only called when the Integration does not yet exist. For an Integration that already exists in the database (created via webhook or a previous partial flow) but whose metadata was stored without a `sender` key — or where `metadata["sender"]` exists but lacks a `login` key — this raises an unhandled `KeyError`, producing a 500 error instead of the intended graceful failure. The code path is reachable: the `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id, status=ObjectStatus.ACTIVE)` at line 494 succeeds for pre-existing integrations, and nothing guarantees `metadata["sender"]["login"]` exists. This should use `.get()` with a safe default (e.g., `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")`) so a missing sender is treated as a mismatch and renders the error page.

Because `PipelineAdvancerView` has `auth_required = False` and `csrf_protect = False` (src/sentry/web/frontend/pipeline_advancer.py lines 25-27), and the pipeline is looked up from a cookie/Redis keyed by pipeline name, an attacker who knows (or guesses) a valid pipeline identifier could craft a request to `sentry-extension-setup` with an arbitrary `installation_id` query parameter. The first request (line 385-387) hits `setup_path` with only `installation_id` — this enters GitHubInstallation (the second pipeline view) which redirects to the GitHub app URL because... actually with the new pipeline, the first view is OAuthLoginView which redirects to GitHub authorize (no state param). The second request (line 388-395) supplies a `state` value of `"ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"` which does NOT match the pipeline signature (`9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3` used elsewhere), so OAuthLoginView returns the generic 'Invalid installation request.' error at the state-mismatch check (integration.py line 412-413) — before any call to `get_installation_info`. The assertion `assert b"Invalid installation request." in resp.content` (line 396) passes, but the test name and the 404 stub are now misleading: the test no longer exercises the 'GitHub installation could not be found' code path in `build_integration` (integration.py lines 352-357). findings.title: assert_setup_flow hardcodes response call index, making it brittle to unrelated stub changes
findings.body: In `assert_setup_flow`, the assertion `auth_header = responses.calls[2].request.headers["Authorization"]` (line 257) relies on the exact ordering and count of HTTP requests made by `responses`. The index was changed from `calls[0]` to `calls[2]` to account for the two new requests made by OAuthLoginView (the token exchange POST and the `/user` GET). This is brittle: any future change that adds or reorders a stubbed HTTP call (e.g., adding a rate-limit check, changing the order of operations in OAuthLoginView, or adding a request in `determine_active_organization`) will silently break this assertion or, worse, assert against the wrong request's headers. findings.title: OAuth access token may be logged or leaked via exception traces
findings.body: In OAuthLoginView.dispatch, the `access_token` obtained from GitHub's token endpoint (line 431-434) is passed to `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])`. If `get_user_info` raises an exception (unhandled, per the related finding), the exception traceback — and potentially the request URL or headers containing the token — could be logged by Sentry's error reporting or appear in server logs. Additionally, the token is stored in the pipeline state only as the derived `login` string (line 438), which is good, but the raw token exists in local variables (`payload`, `data`) for the duration of the request. While this is largely unavoidable in an OAuth flow, the lack of exception handling around `get_user_info` increases the risk that the token-bearing request context is captured in an error report. Wrapping the token-exchange and user-info calls in try/except (returning the generic error page) would prevent token leakage through unhandled exception traces.
